Forward Rate Agreements

Lecture 9 · Fall 2026 · University of San Diego

Rate convention throughout this lecture: all rates are nominal annual rates compounded semiannually. Divide each annual rate by two and compound over twice the number of years.

Fix today the rate on a future loan or investment

Future borrower

You need cash later. Rising rates increase your financing cost.

Future investor

You will have surplus cash later. Falling rates reduce your investment income.

Joined this session 0

Introduction · why future interest rates matter

The problem: we need to borrow later

  • The exposure: a company plans a future investment or payment and will need a loan. It knows the amount and dates, but not the interest rate it will face.
  • Simple example: borrow USD 1 million in 3 months for 6 months. At a 5% annual rate, the expected interest cost is USD 25,000.
  • Rates rise to 7% → bad for the borrower: interest becomes USD 35,000, adding USD 10,000 to the budget.
  • Rates fall to 3% → good for the borrower: interest becomes USD 15,000, saving USD 10,000.
  • The decision today: accept that uncertainty, or use an FRA to fix the benchmark rate for the future period—giving up the benefit of lower rates.

Simple example: annual rates compounded semiannually; one six-month interest period, with no lending spread. The bank brochure below uses its own figures.

Market notation uses months: 3 × 9 means start in 3 months, end in 9 months. The protected period is 6 months.

Motivation · all-class poll

Cash arrives later. Choose the rate today?

A company will receive USD 1 million in ONE year and invest it for TWO years, until year 3.

Option 1 · wait

Wait until year 1. Invest at the 2-year market rate available then. Your interest income is uncertain today.

Option 2 · use an FRA

Fix a 5% nominal annual rate today for years 1–3, compounded semiannually. At year 1, invest at the market rate; the FRA offsets the interest difference.

Everyone votes: At year 1, is 3%, below the 5% . What happens?

Example 1 · future investor

Fix today. Invest in year 1. Finish in year 3.

USD 1 million will be invested for two years. The agreed FRA rate is 5%; the future market rate is unknown today.

Fixed today ·

The rate agreed for the future investment, years 1–3.

Observed at year 1 ·

The market rate on a NEW two-year investment, also years 1–3.

Both rates are nominal annual rates compounded semiannually, covering the same two years. T is the investment length, not the waiting time.
Scenario · future investor

What if the two-year market rate changes?

It is now year 1. Invest USD 1 million until year 3. Compare with the 5% agreed earlier for these same two years.

Activity 1 · 3 points

Investor FRA: calculate the payoff

Payoff at the END of the investment period. Positive: you receive. Negative: you pay. We use the end-period payoff convention in this lecture; no discounting.

Example 2 · future borrower

Borrow next year for one year

A company needs USD 1 million at year 1 and repays at year 2. It fixes a 5% nominal annual rate today using an FRA, with semiannual compounding.

At year 1, compare with on a NEW one-year loan ending in year 2. A higher matching market rate increases the loan cost; the borrower FRA should compensate the company.

What if the one-year market rate changes?

It is now year 1. Borrow USD 1 million until year 2. Compare with the 5% fixed earlier for this same one-year loan.

Wrap-up · same dates, opposite exposures

Who receives the payoff?

Investor · fears lower rates

Market below FRA: receive.
Market above FRA: pay.

Borrower · fears higher rates

Market above FRA: receive.
Market below FRA: pay.

Use the same semiannual compounding for the agreed FRA rate and the matching market rate. Interest accumulates until the end of the period; compare the two final amounts.

Teaching convention: show the undiscounted payoff at the period end. Standard cash-settled FRAs may settle earlier; that adjustment is outside this lecture.
